title: We Already Have Math 2.0. Where is Education 2.0? November 5, 2026
author: Stefan Bauschard
source: Education Disrupted: Teaching and Learning in An AI World (stefanbauschard.substack.com),
summary: Stefan Bauschard takes mathematician Terence Tao's idea of Math 2.0, in which AI changes what mathematicians should do rather than merely speeding up what they already did, and asks what the equivalent would be for schools. He cites Tao's remark that the biggest bottleneck is imagination and his Easter egg hunt example, where teams using AI, software and pen and paper together built a data set of 25,000 polynomials that would have been impractical to collect before. Tao's qualification, that AI should support rather than replace human understanding, anchors Bauschard's argument that revised cheating policies and slightly different assignments are not a sufficient response. He then works through questions about what students should be capable of doing, whether every student needs the same sequence, whether subjects must remain the organizing structure, whether student work could accumulate across years, and whether the boundary between school and the world could soften. He insists that this requires investing in teachers and running serious experiments to see what students actually learn, while keeping foundational knowledge intact.
points: Tao's point that the biggest bottleneck is imagination is turned on schools, which mostly ask whether AI can do the assignments they already set.
The Easter egg hunt shows a mixed method, with AI, software and pen and paper together producing a data set no one could collect before, and AI then used to merge the teams' strategies.
Bauschard accepts Tao's warning that answers without understanding are dangerous, so student projects must still require students to understand and evaluate their results.
He imagines multi-year school projects, such as a local environmental dataset, in which each cohort inherits, critiques and extends earlier work.
He insists change is a staffing and workload question, since teachers need shared planning time and fewer disconnected preparations to design this kind of learning.
quotes: A lot of my colleagues are still focusing on math 1.0 tasks, you know, like trying to publish papers and things, and I think we do have to think beyond that. But the biggest bottleneck is going to be imagination.
We have a technology that is expanding what people can accomplish, but much of our attention remains on whether it can perform the tasks we already recognize and reward.

Notice that this involved a combination of approaches. People used AI, other software, and traditional mathematical reasoning. Together, they assembled something that had previously been impractical to collect.
Use AI not to replace human understanding of what’s going on, but to support it, to strengthen it.

Adding AI to an assignment is a start. Changing the assignment may be necessary. But we should also consider whether the course, the schedule, the curriculum, and the way we define student success still make sense.
The world does not divide its problems into fifty minutes of science, followed by fifty minutes of English, followed by fifty minutes of mathematics.
We cannot simply add those responsibilities to an already full workload. If we want a different educational experience, we have to change the conditions under which teachers work.
If our response to AI ends with revised cheating policies, a few new tools, and slightly different assignments, we will have left the larger opportunity unexplored.
